facts.hermes: Any provider works: Nous Portal (OAuth subscription), OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI/Codex, Google Vertex, xAI, Qwen, MiniMax, Ollama and other local OpenAI-compatible servers. Nous Portal is the recommended route: one OAuth login covers 300+ models plus the Tool Gateway. Bring-your-own keys remain supported per provider. Keys are optional per tool; the README says you can bring your own keys per tool.
facts.openclaw: Bundled provider plugins cover OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, Z.AI, OpenRouter, Amazon Bedrock, xAI, NVIDIA, MiniMax and others; Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio and llama.cpp cover local models. Keys are stored in the auth store or supplied through the Gateway environment; there is no OpenClaw account in the loop.

sources.quote: You need at least one way to connect to an LLM.
Nous Portal is Nous Research's unified subscription gateway and the recommended way to run Hermes Agent.
You can still bring your own keys per-tool whenever you want - the gateway is per-backend, not all-or-nothing.
Model-agnostic: use Anthropic, MiniMax, OpenAI, OpenRouter, etc., with per-agent routing and failover.
Open Settings → Models in the Control UI to add, replace, or remove provider API keys.

facts.hermes: Two files under ~/.hermes/memories: MEMORY.md (2,200 characters, about 800 tokens) and USER.md (1,375 characters, about 500 tokens), injected into the system prompt at session start. Memory is deliberately capped and does not grow without bound; the agent must consolidate or delete entries when full.
facts.openclaw: Memory is plain files on disk; the docs say the limit is your storage, not the model. A pre-compaction flush reminds the model to write durable notes first. Session context is still bounded by the model window, so long conversations compact or truncate.

sources.quote: Hermes Agent has bounded, curated memory that persists across sessions.
Character limits keep memory focused. Memory does not auto-compact: when a write would exceed the limit, the memory tool returns an error instead of silently dropping entries.
OpenClaw memory is Markdown files in the agent workspace: daily notes in memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md, curated long-term notes in MEMORY.md (main/private sessions only).
Memory files live on disk and persist until deleted; the limit is your storage, not the model.

facts.hermes: Skills live in ~/.hermes/skills, follow the agentskills.io standard, and the agent can create, modify or delete them. Bundled, hub-installed and agent-created skills share one directory; MCP servers are the separate plugin route for external tools.
facts.openclaw: Skills are SKILL.md folders with YAML frontmatter, loaded from the workspace or ~/.openclaw/skills, with bundled skills and ClawHub community installs. ClawHub is the community skill registry; plugins are separate packages with their own install and enable commands.

sources.quote: Skills are on-demand knowledge documents the agent can load when needed.
All skills live in ~/.hermes/skills/ - the primary directory and source of truth.
Skills are markdown instruction files that teach the agent how and when to use tools.
Inspect local skills, search ClawHub, install skills from ClawHub/Git/local directories, verify ClawHub skills, and update ClawHub-tracked installs.

facts.hermes: One cronjob_manage tool creates, pauses, edits and removes jobs; jobs can run headless scripts with no model call, deliver to a chat or file, and fire on webhooks. The messaging gateway process owns the scheduler, so scheduled jobs need the gateway running.
facts.openclaw: Jobs persist, wake the agent on a schedule, and deliver to a chat channel, a webhook or nowhere; openclaw automations is the CLI, with openclaw cron as an alias.

sources.quote: Schedule tasks to run automatically with natural language or cron expressions.
The gateway also runs the cron scheduler, ticking every 60 seconds to execute any due jobs.
Automations are OpenClaw's built-in scheduler.

facts.hermes: browser_exec drives a Hermes-packaged Chromium by default; cloud browsers (Nous, Browserbase, Browser Use, Firecrawl) and an attached personal Chrome are alternatives. Computer use runs through the cua-driver MCP server and works with any tool-capable model; it acts on the machine the bot runs on.
facts.openclaw: The managed profile is isolated from the personal browser; an optional user profile attaches to the real signed-in Chrome through Chrome DevTools MCP. macOS uses Peekaboo by default or CUA; Windows and Linux use the experimental cua-computer plugin; a vision-capable model is required.

sources.quote: The browser toolset gives the agent a real web browser.
Hermes Agent can drive your desktop - clicking, typing, scrolling, dragging - in the background on macOS, Windows, and Linux.
OpenClaw can run a dedicated Chrome/Brave/Edge/Chromium profile that the agent controls.
Computer use lets an agent see and control the Gateway's own desktop or a paired node's desktop through one built-in computer tool.

facts.hermes: Access is granted by per-platform user allowlists, Discord role allowlists, a global allowlist or DM pairing codes. Access control is opt-in: an unconfigured gateway refuses everyone, so the owner must add the people who may use the bot. Several people can talk to one bot in a shared channel, each with a separate session. Bot Mode adds several named agents, each with its own memory and credentials.
facts.openclaw: Sessions carry an immutable creator, an assignable owner and participant history, with live presence in the Control UI. Ownership and presence are usability features, not security boundaries; adversarial users need separate gateways.

sources.quote: When running the messaging gateway, Hermes controls who can interact with the bot through a layered authorization system.
If no allowlists are configured and GATEWAY_ALLOW_ALL_USERS is not set, all users are denied.
By default, Hermes isolates session history per user inside the channel for safety and clarity.
Multi-user mode lets several trusted people operate the same OpenClaw agent.
Everyone who can operate an agent can make it do anything that agent can do.

facts.hermes: One-line install.sh for Linux/macOS/WSL2, install.ps1 for Windows, desktop installers (DMG, MSIX), Docker image, Nix flake and modules, Termux APT package for aarch64 Android. The Docker image is stateless and upgraded by pulling a new tag; data lives in the mounted volume.
facts.openclaw: One-line install.sh or install.ps1, npm install -g openclaw@latest, Docker, Nix, and desktop companion apps for macOS and Windows; the installer provisions Node when it is missing. The npm package itself needs Node 24.22.1+ or 26.12.1+, with Node 26 recommended.

sources.quote: Install in 60 seconds on Linux, macOS, WSL2, native Windows, Nix & NixOS or Android
The container stores all user data (config, API keys, sessions, skills, memories) in a single directory mounted from the host at /opt/data.
The installer supports macOS, Linux, and Windows.

facts.hermes: Table on the same page: memory 1 GB minimum, 2-4 GB recommended; CPU 1 core minimum, 2 cores recommended; data disk 500 MB minimum, 2+ GB recommended. Browser use raises the practical memory floor to 2 GB.
facts.openclaw: Same page: recommended 1-2 vCPU and 2 GB+ RAM for headroom; browser automation and multiple channels raise the need. The Fly.io guide uses shared-cpu-2x with 2 GB RAM.

sources.quote: The Hermes container needs moderate resources. Recommended minimums:
Browser automation (Playwright/Chromium) is the most memory-hungry feature. If you don't need browser tools, 1 GB is sufficient. With browser tools active, allocate at least 2 GB.
Absolute minimum: 1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM, ~500 MB disk.
Recommended: 1-2 vCPU, 2 GB+ RAM for headroom (logs, media, multiple channels).

facts.hermes: Layers: user authorization, dangerous-command approval, file-write safety, container isolation, MCP credential filtering, context-file scanning, cross-session isolation and input sanitization. Approvals run in smart, manual or off mode; unattended contexts (cron, webhooks, single-query) deny dangerous commands by default.
facts.openclaw: When enabled, tool execution moves into Docker, Podman, SSH, OpenShell or Crabbox; the Gateway itself always stays on the host. Four modes: read-only, guarded (human review after an allowlist fast path), workspace (LLM review, human on ask) and full, which needs operator.admin. The Gateway binds to loopback, unknown DM senders get a pairing code, and group access is allowlisted behind a mention gate. One gateway is one trust domain; mixed-trust use needs separate gateways and credentials.

sources.quote: The security model has eight layers:
Before executing any command, Hermes checks it against a curated list of dangerous patterns. If a match is found, the user must explicitly approve it.
Sandboxing is off by default and controlled by agents.defaults.sandbox
Session permission modes set one session's filesystem boundary and exec escalation reviewer.
OpenClaw ships with conservative defaults.
OpenClaw is not a hostile multi-tenant security boundary for mutually adversarial users sharing one agent or gateway.

facts.hermes: One Hermes home serves one agent process; a second agent needs its own profile. You cannot bind several profiles to different chats on one WhatsApp number.
facts.openclaw: The docs describe sandboxing as damage limitation, not a hardened boundary. The stock Docker image needs extra build flags to add a browser or system packages.

sources.quote: Don't point two agent processes at the same Hermes home directory.
Current limitation: Hermes profiles each require their own WhatsApp number/session.
This is not a perfect security boundary, but it materially limits filesystem and process access when the model does something dumb.
The default image is security-first and runs as the node user, so it excludes system packages, Homebrew, and bundled browsers.
